Before we can understand frame-dragging, we need two foundational ideas from Einstein's general relativity firmly in place.

Idea 1: Spacetime is a fabric. Space and time are not separate things. They are woven together into a single, unified "fabric" called spacetime. Everything — you, planets, light — exists within this fabric.

Idea 2: Mass curves that fabric. A massive object like the Earth or the Sun doesn't just sit in spacetime — it dents it. Think of a heavy bowling ball placed on a stretched rubber sheet. It sinks in, warping the sheet around it. That warping is gravity. Objects nearby follow the curves of this warped fabric, which is why they orbit or fall.

With that in place, we're ready for frame-dragging.
The Central Question Frame-Dragging Answers

Newtonian gravity — the old model before Einstein — only cared about one thing: how much mass an object has. That's it. A million-ton rock sitting still and a million-ton rock spinning wildly would produce exactly the same gravitational effect on their surroundings according to Newton.

Einstein's general relativity says: not so fast. According to GR, it's not just mass that shapes spacetime — it's moving mass too. And when a massive object rotates, something extraordinary happens. It doesn't just curve the spacetime around it. It also twists it. It literally drags the surrounding fabric of spacetime along with it as it spins, like a spinning object pulling the medium around it.

That twisting, that dragging of spacetime itself — that is frame-dragging.
The Honey Analogy (The Most Intuitive Way to See It)

Imagine spacetime as a very thick, viscous fluid — like honey.

Now take a heavy metal ball and drop it into the honey. It sinks and creates a depression around it. Everything nearby slides toward that depression. That's gravity — the familiar part.

Now make that metal ball spin.

The ball no longer just sits in its depression. As it spins, it grabs the honey immediately around it and swirls it. The faster the ball spins, the more violently the honey swirls. Anything floating nearby gets caught in that swirl — even if it had nothing to do with the spinning ball. Even a tiny foam chip floating in the honey would start rotating, not because of any direct contact, but because the medium itself is rotating around it.

In exactly this way, a rotating massive body — a planet, a star, a black hole — grabs the fabric of spacetime and drags it around with it. Anything in that region of space gets swept along in that rotation, at least partially.
What Is a "Frame," and What Exactly Gets Dragged?

The word "frame" is doing important work here, so let's be precise.

In physics, a frame of reference (or just "frame") is a coordinate system — a kind of imaginary grid you use to measure positions, velocities, and directions. Think of it as the vantage point from which you observe the universe.

A special type of frame is called an inertial frame. This is a frame that is not rotating and not accelerating — a "perfectly neutral" frame where Newton's first law holds: if you put an object at rest and push nothing, it stays at rest. If you spin a gyroscope and let it float freely in space, it points toward the same direction in space forever, because gyroscopes always align with their local inertial frame.

Now here's the key insight:

Far away from any rotating object — say, out among the distant stars — inertial frames are "calm." A freely floating gyroscope out there would point steadily toward some distant star and hold that direction forever.

But get close to a rotating massive body, and those local inertial frames are no longer calm. The rotation of the body twists the local inertial frames themselves. Your gyroscope — which is always loyal to its local inertial frame — starts to slowly precess (change its pointing direction) even though nothing physically touched it or pushed it. It's not the gyroscope that changed; it's the frame itself that got dragged around by the rotating mass.

This is why it's called frame-dragging. The rotating mass drags the inertial frames of spacetime itself.
Who Predicted It, and When?

Frame-dragging is a direct consequence of Einstein's field equations of general relativity, published in 1915. However, the specific effect of a rotating mass dragging nearby spacetime was worked out mathematically by two Austrian physicists, Josef Lense and Hans Thirring, in 1918. Because of this, frame-dragging is also called the Lense-Thirring effect, particularly when referring to the relatively gentle version that occurs around ordinary rotating objects like planets and stars (as opposed to black holes).
A Concrete Example: A Satellite Orbiting Earth

Earth is rotating. It makes one full rotation every ~24 hours. According to general relativity, this rotation is slowly dragging the fabric of spacetime around it — like the spinning honey ball.

Now put a satellite in orbit around Earth with an ultra-precise gyroscope onboard. In a perfectly Newtonian universe, that gyroscope would hold its direction perfectly forever, always pointing at the same distant star.

But because of frame-dragging, Earth's rotation is ever-so-slightly twisting the local spacetime around it. The gyroscope's local inertial frame is being dragged. Over time, the gyroscope slowly, measurably drifts from its original direction — even though nothing physically torques it, bumps it, or touches it.

For Earth, this drift is tiny — about 39 milli-arcseconds per year (0.000011 degrees per year). It's minuscule, but it is real, and it has been measured.
The Gravitomagnetic Analogy: A Deeper Layer

There's a beautiful parallel between frame-dragging and electromagnetism that physicists love.

In electromagnetism:

  • A stationary electric charge creates an electric field that pulls or pushes other charges.
  • A moving electric charge (i.e., an electric current) creates a magnetic field — a fundamentally different kind of field that curves the paths of other moving charges.

The magnetic field is entirely due to the motion of the charge, not the charge's existence alone.

In general relativity, there is a deep analogy:

  • A stationary mass creates a gravitational field — the familiar gravitational attraction.
  • A rotating mass (moving mass) creates a gravitomagnetic field — a fundamentally different component of gravity that is due purely to the motion of the mass.

Frame-dragging is the gravitomagnetic effect. Just as a magnetic field curves the trajectories of moving charges in ways that depend on the direction of their motion relative to the current, the gravitomagnetic field curves the paths and orientations of nearby objects in ways that depend on the direction of their motion relative to the rotating mass. Objects moving in the same direction as the rotation are affected differently from those moving against it.

This isn't just an analogy — mathematically, in the weak-field, slow-speed limit of GR (called gravitoelectromagnetism or GEM), the equations of general relativity map almost perfectly onto Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism, with mass playing the role of charge and the Lense-Thirring effect playing the role of magnetism.
Where Frame-Dragging Becomes Extreme: Rotating Black Holes

Around ordinary objects like Earth or the Sun, frame-dragging is real but subtle. But around a rotating black hole — called a Kerr black hole, after mathematician Roy Kerr who found the exact mathematical solution in 1963 — frame-dragging becomes ferociously powerful.

Around a Kerr black hole, there is a region just outside the event horizon (the "point of no return" boundary of a black hole) called the ergosphere. The name comes from the Greek word ergon, meaning work, because energy can be extracted from this region.

Inside the ergosphere, frame-dragging is so powerful that nothing can remain stationary. Absolutely nothing — not matter, not light, nothing. Even if you fired your rocket engines at full blast in the opposite direction of the black hole's spin, the dragging of spacetime itself would still sweep you around in the direction of the rotation. The entire fabric of spacetime in that region is being whipped around by the black hole's rotation faster than light can "escape" the rotation. Remaining at rest relative to the distant stars becomes physically impossible.

This is a profound statement. It means the black hole's rotation has physically redefined what "stationary" means in that region. There is no such thing as "not rotating" inside the ergosphere.

The Penrose Process: Because of the ergosphere's properties, it's theoretically possible to extract enormous amounts of energy from a rotating black hole. An object can enter the ergosphere, split into two pieces, and if the pieces separate in just the right way, one falls into the black hole while the other flies out with more energy than the original object had. The extra energy comes from the rotational energy of the black hole itself. This is called the Penrose process, after physicist Roger Penrose who proposed it in 1969.
The Effect on Light

Light is not immune to frame-dragging. Near a rotating mass, light beams traveling in the same direction as the rotation and light beams traveling against the rotation experience spacetime differently. Specifically:

  • Light going with the rotation takes a slightly different path than light going against it.
  • Near a rotating black hole, the paths of light are twisted by the dragged spacetime, producing observable effects on things like the bright rings of light seen around black holes (called the photon ring or photon sphere).

In terms of travel time: two light beams sent around a rotating object in opposite directions will arrive back at the same point at slightly different times because one goes "with the flow" of dragged spacetime and one goes against it. This is called the Sagnac effect (though this also has a simpler special-relativistic explanation in flat spacetime).
How Strong Is the Effect Around Ordinary Objects?

To give you a sense of scale:

For a gyroscope in a low Earth orbit (about 650 km above the surface), frame-dragging causes a drift of approximately 39 milli-arcseconds per year. For comparison, the full Moon's apparent size in the sky is about 1,800,000 milli-arcseconds. So the frame-dragging effect on a satellite near Earth is equivalent to a drift of about 1/46,000th of the Moon's diameter per year. Tiny — but real and measurable with precision instruments.

For a neutron star (an incredibly dense, rapidly spinning dead star), the effect is orders of magnitude stronger. For a rotating black hole spinning near its maximum rate, it's enormous — it defines the entire structure of space near it.
Experimental Proof: Gravity Probe B

For decades, frame-dragging was a theoretical prediction of GR that was extremely difficult to measure directly. The breakthrough came with Gravity Probe B, a NASA satellite mission that launched in 2004 and ran until 2011.

Gravity Probe B carried four of the most perfect gyroscopes ever built — quartz spheres coated in a superconducting material, so round that the tallest "mountain" on their surface was only about 40 atoms high. The satellite orbited Earth in a polar orbit, and scientists tracked the direction these gyroscopes pointed over the mission's lifetime with extraordinary precision.

Two effects were measured:

  1. The geodetic effect (a different GR effect due to the curvature of spacetime from Earth's mass, not its rotation) — predicted: −6,606.1 milli-arcseconds/year. Measured: −6,601.8 ± 18.3 milli-arcseconds/year. Confirmed to better than 0.3% accuracy.
  2. The Lense-Thirring frame-dragging effect (due to Earth's rotation) — predicted: −39.2 milli-arcseconds/year. Measured: −37.2 ± 7.2 milli-arcseconds/year. Confirmed to within about 20% accuracy.

Frame-dragging was real. Einstein's prediction from 1915 had been verified directly in the lab of Earth's orbit.

Additional evidence came from the LAGEOS satellites (Laser Geodynamics Satellites), which are metal spheres covered in retroreflectors bouncing laser beams from Earth. By tracking subtle perturbations in their orbits, researchers have confirmed the Lense-Thirring effect from Earth's rotation.
Why Does Frame-Dragging Happen? The Deep "Why"

You might be wondering: why does rotation drag spacetime at all? Here's the deepest answer we can give.

In Einstein's general relativity, spacetime curvature is not produced by mass alone — it's produced by the full stress-energy tensor, which includes energy, momentum, pressure, and stress. A rotating body doesn't just have energy (from its mass and rotational kinetic energy) — it has angular momentum (spinning momentum), which contributes to the momentum terms of the stress-energy tensor.

When Einstein's field equations "see" these momentum terms — the fact that mass is not just sitting there but flowing in a rotational pattern — they produce a component of spacetime curvature that is not purely radial (inward-pulling) but also rotational. It's a twisting of the spacetime geometry that propagates outward from the rotating body, getting weaker with distance but never fully vanishing.

There is also a philosophical connection here to Mach's principle — the idea, which influenced Einstein, that local inertial frames (what "non-rotating" means) are determined by the distribution of all the matter in the universe. Frame-dragging is a partial, local version of this idea: the rotation of a nearby massive body literally reshapes what it means to be "non-rotating" in its vicinity.
Summary: The Complete Picture in Plain Words

Frame-dragging is the phenomenon where a rotating massive object drags the fabric of spacetime itself around with it as it spins. This isn't a metaphor — spacetime near a spinning mass is physically twisted, and anything in that region — gyroscopes, satellites, light, even the very definition of what "stationary" means — gets swept along in that rotation. The effect is tiny near slowly-rotating objects like Earth, but it has been confirmed by precision experiments. Near a rotating black hole, it becomes so powerful that it creates an "ergosphere" where nothing can resist the rotation of spacetime, and from which rotational energy can theoretically be extracted. Frame-dragging is one of the most dramatic demonstrations that in Einstein's universe, matter doesn't just respond to the shape of spacetime — it actively shapes it, and how it moves is just as important as how much of it there is.
